property_summary: After any successful external payment to C via receive(), depositsCount never decreases (reference preserves non-decreasing depositsCount on each receive; mutant that decrements will violate this for some payment),

Every successful call sending Ether to C via its receive() must not decrease depositsCount (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant that decrements depositsCount will violate this for some input value/actor.

For any payable reception that increases the contract balance (nonzero value sent), the depositsCount must never underflow/become less than its previous value; the mutant that decrements depositsCount on receive can reduce depositsCount when a nonzero payment is sent and thus breaks this invariant.

For any address sending a nonzero ether amount to C, the public depositsCount never decreases (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant that decrements on receive can make depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before for some fuzzed amount/actor.

For any address that sends ANY nonzero ether to C via its receive(), depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (i.e., depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant that decrements will violate this for some sender/amount by making depositsCount_after != depositsCount_before + 1.

For any sender and positive amount they send to C's receive (as payable calldata-less transfer), the reference C always increments depositsCount (so a receive call succeeds and increases depositsCount by 1), whereas the mutant always reverts on receive so depositsCount does not increase and the call fails for some inputs.

For any payer address and any positive ETH amount, calling C.receive (a plain payable transfer) never reverts in the reference and increases depositsCount by exactly 1, whereas the mutant always reverts; the test asserts that after a payable transfer depositsCount == 1 and the call succeeded.

For any sender and positive ETH amount, sending ETH to C via a contract that forwards the payment (so C's receive executes with a non-empty msg.sender that is a contract) always succeeds and increments depositsCount by 1 in the reference, whereas the mutant's receive always reverts and thus fails for some such forwarding callers.

For any call to receive that sends value (any nonzero wei), the reference contract guarantees depositsCount increments by 1 and thus (depositsCount_new >= depositsCount_old); the mutant without the require can be forced (by sending 0 wei) to produce the same increment behavior but violate the intended monotonic non-decreasing guard for edge cases—specifically, the correct contract prevents wrapping/illegal decrement effects by requiring (depositsCount+1)>=depositsCount for every deposit, while the mutant removes that guard and can break the general monotonicity property for some fuzzed inputs.

After any payable receive call, the depositsCount reported by the contract never decreases (depositsCount_new >= depositsCount_old); the mutant removal of the require allows a scenario where this monotonic, non-decreasing property can be violated for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller and any wei value sent to receive, the reference contract guarantees depositsCount increases by exactly 1 after a successful receive call (depositsCount_new == depositsCount_old + 1); the mutant that removes the require can be forced (via a reentrant attacker that reenters during receive) to make depositsCount diverge from this +1 invariant.

For any single successful external payable call to receive (from any caller sending any nonnegative wei), depositsCount never decreases (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); removing the require can allow a malicious reentrant caller to make depositsCount wrap/behave such that this non-decreasing property is violated for some input.

For any address and any wei amount sent to C via its receive (as a payable external call), the reference contract always increases depositsCount by exactly 1 (depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant that removed the require can be forced (by sending 0 wei from any caller) to violate this invariant for some inputs.

For every single payable call to receive, the reference C increments depositsCount by exactly 1 (so depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant increments by 2 for some inputs, violating this invariant.
For any caller sending a nonzero Ether amount to C via its receive() the contract's depositsCount increases by exactly 1; the mutant increments it by 2 for some inputs, violating that invariant.
Only the owner can successfully call withdrawAll (i.e., withdrawAll reverts when called by any non-owner caller).
Calling withdrawAll should succeed (not revert) when invoked by the contract owner.
The test asserts that calling c.withdrawAll() from this contract does not revert (i.e., reverted == false).

Rule: only the owner can successfully invoke owner-restricted functions (owner can withdraw all funds); the mutant inverts the check so non-owners can call owner-only functions — causing owner-privileged effects (like withdrawAll reducing contract balance) to be possible only when caller != owner (breaking the rule).

The contract invariant: only the deployer (owner) can invoke owner-restricted actions that transfer Ether out of the contract; the mutant inverts the check so a non-owner caller can perform those transfers, allowing a non-owner call to reduce the contract balance while the owner cannot.

For every address caller and value, only the contract owner (the deployer) can cause owner-restricted withdrawals that reduce the contract balance; the mutant inverts the ownership check so a non-owner can perform those withdrawals, allowing a non-owner call to reduce the contract balance while the owner cannot.

For any caller and value, only the contract owner (deployer) can cause the contract balance to decrease via withdrawAll/sendMoney flows; the mutant inverts onlyOwner so a non-owner can trigger balance-reducing withdrawals, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller who is the owner and for any contract balance >= 1 wei, calling withdrawAll empties the contract balance (withdraws the entire balance); the mutant subtracting 1 wei causes the contract to retain 1 wei for some balances and thus violates this rule.

For any owner-funded balance >= 1 wei, calling withdrawAll will transfer the entire contract balance out (leaving address(c).balance == 0) in the reference C; the mutant that calls withdraw(address(this).balance - 1) can leave 1 wei in the contract for some balances, violating this rule.

For any caller who is owner and any initial contract balance that is an odd number >= 1 wei, calling withdrawAll transfers the entire balance out (leaving address(c).balance == 0) in the reference, but the mutant that subtracts 1 wei from address(this).balance can leave 1 wei behind and thus violate this for some balances.

For any owner caller and any initial contract balance B >= 1, calling withdrawAll always results in the contract balance decreasing by exactly B (i.e. address(c).balance == 0) in the reference; the mutant that calls withdraw(address(this).balance - 1) can leave 1 wei in the contract for some B, violating this.

For any owner caller and any initial contract balance of 0, calling withdrawAll must revert (because withdraw(address(this).balance) tries to withdraw 0 which is a no-op but withdrawAll on zero balance should still attempt to call withdraw(0) — we assert that the call does NOT succeed for zero balance), while the mutant that subtracts 1 from balance will underflow/behave differently and cause a revert difference for some inputs.

For all callers and contract balances, calling withdrawAll on the correct contract always routes the contract balance through the withdraw(...) function (so external callee behavior invoked by withdraw can affect outcome); the mutant that directly transfers to owner bypasses withdraw and therefore behaves differently when the owner address is a contract whose receive/fallback reverts (the reference will propagate that failure via withdraw while the mutant will attempt a direct transfer to owner and thus may revert or succeed differently).

For any recipient contract with a reverting fallback/receive and any deposited balance, calling withdrawAll on the correct C routes the payout through withdraw (which performs a low-level call that does not revert on recipient revert), so withdrawAll never reverts and reduces C's balance to 0; the mutant that uses payable(owner).transfer(...) will revert when owner is a reverting contract and thus breaks this rule for some inputs.

For any beneficiary contract that may revert on receiving Ether and for any deposit amount, the reference C's withdrawAll() always completes and reduces C's balance to 0 (because it calls withdraw which uses transfer to msg.sender after going through withdraw path that in reference uses call semantics allowing the external behaviour to be handled), whereas the mutant that uses payable(owner).transfer(...) can revert or behave differently when owner is a reverting contract—so the invariant that withdrawAll() does not revert and leaves C balance zero is broken by the mutant for some inputs.

For any deposit amount and any owner address that is a contract which reverts on receiving ETH, calling withdrawAll on the correct contract always completes (does not revert) and leaves the contract balance at zero, but the mutant that does payable(owner).transfer(...) may revert (so the property is violated for some inputs).

For any owner contract that accepts ether (non-reverting), after depositing some ether and calling withdrawAll as the owner, the reference C always reduces its balance to zero (funds are forwarded via withdraw) whereas the mutant that directly uses payable(owner).transfer(...) may behave differently for some inputs; the test checks that withdrawAll completes and leaves address(c).balance == 0 for all fuzzed deposits and owner choices that are contracts that accept ether.

For any caller, only the contract owner can reduce the contract balance via withdrawAll (i.e., calling withdrawAll does not change address(c).balance unless msg.sender==owner); the mutant removing onlyOwner allows some non-owner caller to drain balance, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller that is not the contract owner, calling withdrawAll must not decrease address(c).balance (only owner can withdraw); the mutant removing onlyOwner allows a non-owner caller to drain the balance for some inputs.

For any caller who is NOT the contract owner and for any initial balance, calling withdrawAll must revert (or at least not succeed in withdrawing) under the reference because withdrawAll is owner-only; the mutant removing onlyOwner allows a non-owner to successfully withdraw the contract balance for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any non-owner caller and any nonzero contract balance funded via receive(), calling withdrawAll must not change the contract's balance when executed by that caller under the reference (it will only succeed for the owner); the mutant that removes onlyOwner allows some non-owner caller to decrease address(c).balance for some fuzzed caller and amount.

For any non-owner caller and any funded contract balance, calling withdrawAll must NOT succeed in transferring the contract balance (the call either reverts due to onlyOwner or has no effect); removing onlyOwner allows some non-owner to successfully withdraw and thus decrease address(c).balance.
Only the original owner can withdraw contract balance, so a non-owner call to withdraw does not decrease the contract balance.
withdraw(...) reverts for any caller who is not the contract's owner (i.e., non-owner cannot successfully call withdraw).
If the provided caller address is not the contract's owner, then invoking withdraw should revert (i.e., caller == c.owner() or the withdraw call from this contract reverts).
If the caller argument is not the owner of c, then calling withdraw should revert (i.e., caller == c.owner() || reverted).
If the provided caller address is not the contract's owner, then invoking withdraw should revert (i.e., caller == c.owner() || reverted).
